findings[27].title.en: 24 closed tasks have no dev_history; the “one file per task” convention is broken

findings[27].evidence.en: 149 non-epics in Jira, 119 keys present in the filenames under docs/dev_history/. 31 have no file, 7 of them in To Do → 24 closed with no history: GSL-30; GSL-113…131 (except 118/122/123); GSL-112 and 133–138 are folded into a single epic file, contrary to the README's “One file per Jira Task”.

findings[27].means.en: The self-documenting laboratory is silent about a quarter of recent tasks. Meanwhile the coverage metric counts by its own rules and shows no discrepancy.

findings[27].recommendation.en: Decide explicitly whether one summary file per epic is acceptable (then write it into the README and teach the metric to count it), or back-fill. The latter is more expensive and unnecessary for 16 one-line UI findings.

findings[27].calibration.en: The red team: the spot check agreed.

findings[28].title.en: The reports describe a two-week-old system and carry no validity date

findings[28].evidence.en: loop-engineering/index.html, verbatim: “Missing — self-pulse, auto-restart-after-death, question buffer, night mode, dynamic wake pacing” — all of it built by epics GSL-49/65/72 (PR #66, #82, #92). None of the five reports carries a validity banner; their internal dates stop at 2026-07-08…07-10.

findings[28].means.en: The project's most visible artefact misleads its reader about the state of the project itself. This is not the authors' mistake — it is the absence of a rule saying that a report goes stale.

findings[28].recommendation.en: Add a “data correct as of; see this link for what changed” header to every report, and put the requirement into the PRD's Reporting section.

findings[28].calibration.en: The red team did not reproduce this (it requires a line-by-line comparison of four HTML files).

findings[29].title.en: The economic premise about claude -p was carried into the PRD as a hard invariant with no note about its source

findings[29].evidence.en: PRD:64 — “claude -p is billed from the programmatic credit pool”. The source (headless-and-supervision) says of itself: “CAVEAT — the dollar figures are secondary-source. The primary Help-Center text was not directly retrievable”. Anthropic's live primary source, fetched 2026-07-24: “Update June 15: We're pausing the changes… For now, nothing has changed: claude -p… still draw from your subscription's usage limits”.

findings[29].means.en: A cross-cutting constraint that shapes the architecture of all six phases was derived from an unverified claim. If it is wrong, some decisions were taken for nothing.

findings[29].recommendation.en: Rewrite C3 with an explicit confidence marker and a requirement to re-check the live source before any decision that leans on billing.

findings[29].calibration.en: The red team fetched the primary source itself. Correction: “paused”, not “cancelled” — a pause is not a cancellation and can be lifted.

findings[30].title.en: claude -p works on this machine on the subscription — measured, not repeated second-hand

findings[30].evidence.en: claude -p “reply with the single word: pong” --output-format json → exit 0, result “pong”, modelUsage claude-opus-5[1m], provider firstParty, contextWindow 1000000. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY not set, ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN not set. Reproduced independently by the red team.

findings[30].means.en: A door the project believed half-closed is open. Headless needed no API key at all — subscription authentication works.

findings[30].recommendation.en: Stop treating -p as forbidden, but do not make it the main engine either: its correct role is a rare, one-off judgement after the mechanical layer has found an anomaly.

findings[30].calibration.en: Three independent routes to one conclusion. Which pool it is billed against is not proven — that requires /usage in the owner's live session.

findings[31].title.en: The price of one claude -p call: $0.30 with zero cache reuse

findings[31].evidence.en: The red team's measurement: total_cost_usd = 0.30081, cache_creation_input_tokens = 30060, cache_read = 0. The first auditor's measurement: two calls at 0.2309 and 0.1993 with a 19–22 thousand token warm-up.

findings[31].means.en: A supervisor polling the system every 3 minutes would cost about $6 an hour and roughly $48 for an eight-hour night — out of the same pool the fleet works from. Our shell watchdog costs exactly zero tokens.

findings[31].recommendation.en: Forbid polling through -p explicitly. Its correct role is a single call, once the mechanical layer has already detected an anomaly and someone needs to read the ledger and decide whether this is a stall or a legitimate pause.

findings[31].calibration.en: The red team raised this from MINOR to MAJOR: it is not a footnote but the decisive argument.

findings[32].title.en: Pulse cadence and the semantics of context_pct disagree with our own skill

findings[32].evidence.en: 199 heartbeat intervals: 15 (7 %) inside the 300–540 s zone the skill forbids; 114 (57 %) above the watchdog's threshold. context_pct equals exactly 98 in 140 lines while cycle stays at 81 and open_workers at 0; the last lines of the same file read 18/19/22. status “quiesced” — 0 records, even though periods with zero workers lasted more than two days.

findings[32].means.en: The signal the watchdog is supposed to judge the orchestrator's health by is unreliable. Switched on as-is, the watchdog would either demand a roll constantly or constantly conclude that the orchestrator has hung.

findings[32].recommendation.en: Fix the semantics of context_pct in one sentence in the skill (consumed, not remaining), add quiesced to the chain-completion checklist, and reconcile WD_HB_STALE_SECS with the real cadence.

findings[32].calibration.en: The red team corrected two numbers: exactly 98 in 140 lines (not 178), and 15 intervals in the zone (not 14).

findings[33].title.en: The pulse cadence contradicts the owner's order (WITHDRAWN: there is no contradiction)

findings[33].evidence.en: SKILL.md:310 — “Dead zone >=300s and <540s — NEVER… ‘I'll check in 5 minutes' (300s) is exactly this trap”; repeated in the Quick reference at :949. Standing rules: “2026-07-07 (owner, IN FORCE): PULSE ~5-10 min with a live fleet”. The economic justification for the prohibition rests on a five-minute prompt-cache TTL; in the current harness the TTL is an hour (confirmed by the synthesiser against the planning tool's documentation).

findings[33].means.en: 540 seconds is nine minutes — inside the owner's 5–10 minute window; the skill explicitly notes that “540s itself is the stable-waiting floor, not the zone”. Decisively: the owner's own lesson file, orchestrator-pulse-rule.md, prescribes the SAME 270 and 540 seconds with the same justification. The skill does not argue with the rule — it is the rule's operational transcription.

findings[33].recommendation.en: All that remains is that the economic justification is out of date (a five-minute cache TTL against today's hour) — MINOR. Importantly: the skill AND the owner's lesson file went stale together, both standing on the same physics.

findings[33].calibration.en: Downgraded by the synthesiser from CRITICAL to MAJOR: the practical cost is extra turns or a late reaction, not a breakage. COLLAPSED ENTIRELY. Calibration evidence over 200 pulses: the median with a live fleet is 594 seconds (inside the owner's window), with 16 % of ticks in the “dead zone”. The claim that “the orchestrator must break one of two rules on EVERY pulse” is refuted by direct measurement. The cause of the error: the auditor read the MEMORY.md index rather than the lesson file itself, and the synthesiser inherited that.

findings[34].title.en: The demand to roll at 70 percent context contradicts the owner's HARD rule

findings[34].evidence.en: SKILL.md:729 (“at ~70% … roll at a clean boundary”), :221 (context_pct is a mandatory heartbeat field, “the watchdog compares it to the roll ceiling”). Standing rules: “2026-07-20 (owner, HARD): do NOT roll on a self-estimate of context… the premature roll at 12:17Z was called a serious mistake”.

findings[34].means.en: The skill pushes the orchestrator towards exactly the action the owner dissected as an incident. Worse: a roll requires terminating every worker, so a mistaken roll also kills the live fleet.

findings[34].recommendation.en: Replace the self-estimate threshold with “roll only on a real harness signal or an owner instruction, and only if a successor mechanically exists”; keep context_pct as an informational field, not a trigger.

findings[34].calibration.en: Downgraded by the synthesiser from CRITICAL to MAJOR: a compensating control exists — the Standing rules live in STATE, which the orchestrator reads at startup, and there has been no recurrence since 20 July. DOWNGRADED from CRITICAL to MAJOR. The aggravating factor the auditor added (“a mistaken roll kills the live fleet”) is WRONG: the same skill forbids killing a productive worker for a roll three separate times (“There is no roll now and deal with the worker later”). Empirically: context_pct >= 70 in 171 of 200 pulses with only ONE rolling status — so the prediction “it will inevitably fall into a roll” is false; the orchestrator reads STATE as well. This is one of the TWO genuine contradictions with the owner's orders.

findings[35].title.en: The skill demands a telemetry line from the worker but never documents the method

findings[35].evidence.en: The tokens_out/tokens_in/cache_read requirement — SKILL.md:770, 966, 989, 991; worker-cycle-template:171. The ban on transcripts — SKILL.md:135, 976, 1002. Recovering the numbers “from the ORCHESTRATOR REPORT block” presumes that a dead worker wrote down figures it could never have seen.

findings[35].means.en: The “unexecutable” claim is refuted: the method is permitted and used daily. What remains is real: a naive worker does not know where to get the numbers and will write UNRECOVERED, or invent them.

findings[35].recommendation.en: Legitimise the method that works: the orchestrator reads usage from the worker's JSONL transcript, located by the brief's code phrase, and writes the telemetry line itself. This is exactly what the project does today by hand.

findings[35].calibration.en: Downgraded by the synthesiser from CRITICAL to MAJOR: the observable harm is corrupted reporting data, not stopped work. DOWNGRADED from CRITICAL to MINOR. The claim that “the only working method is forbidden by the skill itself” is REFUTED: the ban on reading a transcript is addressed to the ORCHESTRATOR and concerns a WORKER's transcript (all nine occurrences checked); nobody ever forbade a worker its own transcript. The method works — the telemetry for cycles 104/107/110 contains real numbers. And the red team found the REAL root of the ~14000-style estimates, which the auditor missed: an internal contradiction in the skill, where SKILL.md:965 permits “even if token counts are approximate” against :771 “NEVER fabricate an aggregate”.

findings[36].title.en: The steps.log watchdog for the verifier is not implemented anywhere

findings[36].evidence.en: SKILL.md:137-147 requires a background observer polling steps.log every ~20 s. grep steps.log tools/watchdog/watchdog.sh → 0; there are no steps.log files in the tree.

findings[36].means.en: Incident E17 (an hour-long pipeline hang on the browser) is closed only by the instruction “the orchestrator starts the verifier itself”. The promised early hang detector is a fiction; the actual reaction ceiling remains a crude 20-minute timer.

findings[36].recommendation.en: Either implement the observer as a small bash poller, or replace the requirement with something executable: a mandatory PROGRESS report from the verifier every N steps.

findings[36].calibration.en: Not reviewed by a red team. DOWNGRADED: the protection against incident E17 rests not on a poller but on a change of process owner — the verifier is started by the ORCHESTRATOR in a separate pane (VERIFY-REQUEST), and that is marked as a live-validated default. A steps.log poller shortens the reaction from 20 minutes to 3; it is not the only barrier.

findings[37].title.en: The worker limit in the tmux skill is four times too high

findings[37].evidence.en: The skill: “pane limit per session: usually ~16… warn at >=14”. The memory file teammate-spawn-cap.md: the fourth concurrent teammate fails with “fork failed: Device not configured”. Manifest section 5: slots max 3. Briefing 48: fleet cap 3.

findings[37].means.en: These are different quantities being compared, not an overstatement: the skill records an observation from 13 July (the 17th spawn failed with 16 IDLE panes), the memory file one from 7 July (the 4th CONCURRENT LIVE teammate failed).

findings[37].recommendation.en: The recommendation “replace the number with 3” is HARMFUL: the skill is global, and on another machine three would be as much a lie as sixteen. The correct edit is “the ceiling is machine-specific, established by experience, and recorded in the project's STATE”.

findings[37].calibration.en: Not reviewed by a red team. DOWNGRADED. The memory file itself says, word for word, “the cap is in the harness/agent-spawn path, not tmux itself” and “Verify the cap still holds before relying on it”. The prediction “it will waste several turns on diagnosis” does not survive scrutiny: the skill quotes the error text verbatim.

findings[38].title.en: The tmux skill recommends killing every foreign pane by default

findings[38].evidence.en: Section 6 — “do NOT kill an active worker's pane… a pane of unknown purpose”; section 9 — “Kill them all with the batch pattern… Recommended by default” before a roll.

findings[38].means.en: At a session boundary the skill advises exactly the action it calls an orphan risk a few screens earlier, and which the main skill forbids with a HARD gate.

findings[38].recommendation.en: Remove the batch pattern as a default recommendation; keep “terminate by name after a confirmed COMPLETE”.

findings[38].calibration.en: Not reviewed by a red team. Related to the incident of 2026-07-07, when kill-pane -a killed a live fleet. DOWNGRADED: section 9 refers to the batch pattern in section 6, and that one carries the applicability condition “all workers idle-freed”; the section 9 scenario is also about idle panes. “Directly breaks” is an overstatement. The genuine narrow defect: the pattern does not exclude a pane of UNKNOWN purpose. Formally the pattern complies with the owner's rule of 7 July.

findings[39].title.en: The Workflow tool is permitted to the orchestrator by the skill and forbidden by the owner

findings[39].evidence.en: SKILL.md:885 — “Workflow → orchestrator-authored bounded fan-out. Use ONLY for one-off preflight audits”; lifecycle E9 — “launch important audits from the orchestrator level”. Standing rules — “2026-07-01 (owner, IN FORCE): NO Workflow tool. Every agent = a tmux-pane teammate”. Manifest section 6 repeats the error by limiting the ban to workers only.

findings[39].means.en: The owner's rule itself contains a permitting path — “Ask before any Workflow”. The genuine defect is that the skill lacks the “ask the owner” gate, not that “the skill overturns a ban”.

findings[39].recommendation.en: A five-word insertion at line 885. This is the second of the TWO genuine contradictions.

findings[39].calibration.en: Not reviewed by a red team. DOWNGRADED. Half the evidence is a misreading: E9 says “launch important audits from the orchestrator level”, which is about the LEVEL, not the tool; with Workflow banned that means a teammate pane started by the orchestrator. The worker layer, meanwhile, is closed off firmly both in the skill and in delivery-workflow.

findings[40].title.en: The skill's model policy has been rescinded by the owner; three sources give three different versions

findings[40].evidence.en: SKILL.md:846 — “orchestrator premium, workers mid, ALL verification cheap tier”; manifest section 2 — “Fable 5 / Opus 4.8”; Standing rules 2026-07-24 — “Opus 5 is out — the new orchestrator and ALL workers run on Opus 5”. In practice, STATE telemetry shows: 64 cycles on claude-opus-4-8, 32 on claude-fable-5, 3 on claude-opus-5 — the three-tier policy was not being followed anyway.

findings[40].means.en: An orchestrator reading only the skill will put verification on a cheap model, against a direct order.

findings[40].recommendation.en: Keep the principle in the skill (the tier is set by the owner, model is always explicit, never trust a model's self-report — check the transcript) and keep the specific models in one place: the manifest.

findings[40].calibration.en: Two independent confirmations. DOWNGRADED and reclassified: this is staleness, not an order to break a rule. The skill is dated 10 July, the rule the 24th, and the owner changed the policy FOUR TIMES in seventeen days. Text written before a rule cannot order that rule to be broken. The operational rule “ALWAYS pass model: explicitly” is correct and in force.

findings[41].title.en: The tmux-agents-orchestration skill does not exist in the repository at all

findings[41].evidence.en: find skill -type f → orchestrating, delivery-workflow, handoff, using-jira, writing-prds, remote-control; tmux-agents-orchestration is absent. The file exists only as ~/.claude/skills/tmux-agents-orchestration/SKILL.md (13,993 bytes, mtime 13 July).

findings[41].means.en: The knowledge from the 13 July incident (16 live panes → fork failed) is not under version control, not backed up and not reviewed. Losing the Claude Code profile means losing the skill entirely.

findings[41].recommendation.en: On the owner's instruction, perform a one-off reverse sync global → skill/ and commit it; add the skill to skill/README.md and CLAUDE.md.

findings[41].calibration.en: Not reviewed by a red team. The finding is unique — nobody else made it.

findings[42].title.en: The project has no agreed list of its own skills

findings[42].evidence.en: CLAUDE.md — “source of truth for all 5 owned skills”, the fifth being writing-prds; skill/README.md — the same 5 plus the instruction “run ./install.sh after any edit”; in fact skill/ holds 6 folders and the global profile 7; briefing 48 names tmux-agents-orchestration as the fifth.
